newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans say its time to prepare for euro.
newsitem.headline: Germans say its time to prepare for euro.

text.p: German politicians and journalists on Sunday hailed the government for finalising the "stability pact" for Europe's planned single currency and said it was time to prepare the country for losing its beloved mark.

They stressed that while the stability pact would help reassure the German public that the future euro would be stable and credible, the most important thing remained to convince the public that the new currency will be as strong as the mark.
One more pessimistic commentator said the government should have held a referendum to allow Germans the chance to voice their own opinion on the single currency.
Germans have a deep fear of inflation and will only exchange their marks for a currency with rock-solid guarantees of long-term stability.
The positive editorials and statements continued a weekend of praise for Chancellor Helmut Kohl, giving him a boost in his fight to reassure citizens worried about giving up the mark.
Colour pictures of the new notes, which have been well received by the press, have featured on the front pages of newspapers over the weekend.
On Saturday Bild, Germany's biggest-selling daily, said the designs had made the currency "beautiful, really European."

Correspondents and commentators from newspapers and television rallied behind the agreement struck in Dublin, which lays down sanctions and fines for countries which take part in monetary union but then fail to meet annual budget targets.
"This pact is doubtless an important step forwards and a great victory for Finance Minister Theo Waigel," said the popular Bild am Sonntag in a commentary.
But it warned "Whoever takes the mark away from the Germans, without giving them a euro which is just as strong, will lose the election in 1998."

The praise could scarcely have come at a better time for Kohl, the driving force behind European integration, who has found his compatriots increasingly anxious about giving up their beloved rock-hard national currency.
Just a few days ago, a survey found 61 percent of Germans looked forward with fear to economic and monetary union (EMU) while only 16 percent were hopeful about the euro currency.

The Frankfurter Allgemeine Sunday edition was cautious saying: "The introduction of a common currency doesn't warm (the German people's) hearts but fills them with the worry that a weaker euro will take the place of their strong mark."

Sunday's edition of the Leipziger Volkszeitung said: "A real, common Europe will collapse if the finance minister undermines the citizens' trust in a safe currency through sleight of hand. Making sure it doesn't come to that is more important than beautiful new notes."
On The Press Club, a round table Sunday afternoon discussion with journalists and experts, opinion was divided over how the euro would compare with the mark.
"Very, very many people will be happy holding this money in their hand," said Hans-Peter Martin of Spiegel magazine.

But economist Wilhelm Hankel said: "Such an important decision as getting rid of the Deutschemark should have been put to a referendum...If the government had courage it would have put it to the people."

Lorenz Wolff of Stern magazine said the most important thing was to prepare people for the currency reform. "The German government has made one big mistake which is not to have provided a clear explanation of what the euro would mean up until now."
